name: Ameren
headline: A regulated electric and gas utility with a published, growing base of plant it earns a set return on.
what_short: Regulated electric and gas utility, Missouri and Illinois
what_it_does: Ameren sells electricity and natural gas to homes and businesses in Missouri and Illinois, and owns high-voltage transmission lines. Regulators in those states and at the federal level set the return it may earn on the plant it builds. It plans $30.5 to $33.1 billion of capital spending from 2026 to 2030.
why_it_passed: Its economics are easy to foresee: the allowed returns are written in rate orders (for example 8.72% on equity at Ameren Illinois electric distribution and 10.48% for federal transmission).
The company publishes its plant-building plan five years ahead, so the growth in its earning base is knowable.
The return on the equity slice of its capital has been 10.1% to 11.4% in every year from 2018.
The analysis found no wildfire-type liability in its filings and judged management honest.
why_not_now: A regulator caps what Ameren may earn, so the price is far above what that capped return justifies. At $106.08 a share against a value range of $18.84 to $36.89, a buyer would earn only about 2.9% to 3.9% a year on the cash the business produces, less than a 30-year US Treasury bond (5.43%).
watch: Debt is 60% of its capital (52% in 2016), and it must raise new debt and sell new shares every year to fund the building plan.
Without leverage the business earns roughly the long bond rate on its capital (about 6% a year).
Coal still supplied 56.5% of Ameren Missouri's energy in 2025, and a plant was retired early after a court found Clean Air Act violations.
